timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Hi, I'm the Ashruget and I've managed to get my new pantry camera out on the telescope and capture first light with it.
So in this video, I'm going to show you how I went through the process of putting everything together to achieve the back focus as you're on screen here.
And the resulting images I managed to capture and it was a little bit of a journey, but we got there in the end.
So one of the biggest issues that I faced was achieving back focus.
The ZS81 or the ZS81 from William Optics, which is my telescope.
It is a refractor and it has per this diagram 150.05 mil of back focus, which is quite a lot.
This is without a feel flat nor a reduced in place.

So one of the things that I had to do was make sure that I had enough spaces in place in conjunction with using the focus for itself to reach that 15 centimeters or 150 mil before the camera sensor sits at that on that plane.
Now, that was further pushed back a little bit by the introduction of our Barlow.
So refractors, they don't have the greatest focal length or certainly this one doesn't have the greatest.
So for particularly for planetary, it's not an ideal telescope, but for lunar, it works quite well.
And that's what I chose to do because the planets aren't at the best position for imaging at this time of the year.
So the way I achieved back focus was with a bit of trial and error.
And I set it up during the day to test it out on a neighbor's roof about about five, six hours away from mine, just to get it as close as I could.
So this is what I ended up with.
I had basically the telescope focuser out a fairly decent amount.
And then I added in a bunch of extenders, which I'd attached to a part of my module of Barlow.
So I used the bad of Hyperion module of Barlow and I just took the front, the front piece off there.
And that's what I inserted into the focuser itself.
And then attach that directly to the camera.
So the 150 mil is kind of split between the two.
So it got partially made up of the extenders and then partially based on the focuser on the telescope itself.
Now the Barlow pushed it back further, so I did end up going beyond the 150.
But it was close enough to get me started.
So once I managed to sort out all of those issues, then I was able to get to imaging and the seeing wasn't great.
So you'll be able to see in these videos that the kind of atmosphere was a bit wobbly.
And that did have an impact on the resulting images that I could produce.
But at least I managed to get the camera out there, try it out and see what it could produce.
And the results for particularly the second image that I'm going to show, I was very happy with.
The first one, not so much, but by that point, like the weather, it really wasn't conducive to a good high quality precise image.
The moon was dipping.
The atmosphere, it was quite windy and it really didn't help the situation.
So I'm going to try again later in the year.
I'll try it on planetary.
I'll also be trying it throughout course of the year on some lunar imaging if I get some clear nights.
And I'll be sharing those results with you.
But for the time being, I'm pretty happy with the camera itself.
It's clearly capable of producing some really high quality images.
It's just down to finding the right nights as with all things astrophysically.
So that's it for this video.
And I want to share this.
Couple of images from the moon with you.
I hope you enjoyed it.
If you did, please consider giving the video a like and subscribe to the channel if you're not already.
And I will catch you next time.
Thanks for watching.

youtube_description:
After patiently waiting for almost three months, clear(ish) skies finally arrived and presented me with an opportunity to capture first light with the ASI 662mc planetary camera!

Join me as I briefly talk through my setup, how I achieved the required back focus using my refractor and captured a couple of lunar images. 

Clear skies!

#astrophotography #zwo #asi662mc #zs81 #williamoptics
youtube_title: ASI 662MC: Finding Back Focus & FIRST LIGHT!
